psychotherapeutic intervention in anxiety disorders results in a decrease of activity in limbic brain structures, and that psycho- and pharmacotherapeutic effects in these disorders share commonalities.

CBT in OCD leads to decreased metabolism in the caudate nucleus and that CBT in phobia leads to decreased activity in limbico-paralimbic areas and that these effects resemble those of SSRIs in these diseases.

the neurobiological effects of psychotherapy are still largely unknown.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the brain is not a passive recipient of psychotherapy, but that psychotherapy is a dynamic process that can change the brain in a variety of ways.
functional neuroimaging has already contributed to the understanding of the mechanisms underlying psychotherapy effects and will continue to do so in the near future.
the neurobiological mechanisms of psychological interventions have been clarified to an extent that they can be used in the development of novel psychotherapeutic strategies.
The main takeaway from our work is that

functional imaging can provide important information on the mechanisms through which psychotherapy exerts its effects and can be used as an important tool for the development of new psychotherapy protocols.
psychotherapy changes the way the brain functions and that this change is not only reflected in clinical outcome.
